transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (CTO, Cerulean), Liam O'Connor (Sr ML Eng), Nora Feldman (Cloud Infra), Arjun Patel (PM)

Summary: Initial scouting call to align on model selection (open models), context length needs (multi-sequence and document retrieval workflows), multilingual support, and tool-calling. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs and compliance needs. Agreed on next steps to exchange security docs and run a dedicated PoC for 8k/32k contexts with tool-calling.

Topics: model options, context length, multilingual, tool-calling, VPC/KMS, performance SLOs, pricing/bursting, benchmarks

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. We're here to understand your use case and constraints, and then map out model and deployment options — hosted, dedicated, or private VPC.
[00:16] Priya: Thanks Maya. Quick intro from our side — I'm Priya, CTO, and Liam, Nora, Arjun are on. We run a knowledge retrieval assistant across docs and ticketing, multilingual across EN/FR/ES and occasional JA. Latency SLO is about 400 ms p95 for short responses, but for long doc summarization we can accept higher.
[00:33] Liam: Our biggest pain is cost at scale — we've tried few-shot OpenAI and also some open self-hosted weights. The cost of tokens for heavy summarization kills margins. Also tool-calling is mission critical: we call a vector store and internal indexing microservices.
[00:50] Diego: Got it. A few clarifying q's — what's your average context length for the retrieval augmented generation (RAG) path? Are you concatenating many docs into a single prompt or using chunked retrieval?
[01:06] Arjun: We chunk; typical active context is 3-7 chunks, each 1-2k tokens. But for onboarding flows we sometimes send whole long threads ~20k tokens. So we need support for both 8k and 32k windows ideally.
[01:23] Priya: Correct. Also multilingual quality: FR and ES must be good, and JA is lower volume. We prefer open models but are flexible if redwood has a sweet spot for cost/perf.
[01:37] Maya: Perfect. High level: Hosted gives fastest time to value and simplest ops, Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) gives predictable throughput and isolation with capacity commitments, and Private/VPC gives you customer-managed network + KMS / HSM for keys — useful for tighter compliance. We can run the same API and routing policies across all.
[01:56] Nora: On compliance, we need SOC2 type II, audit logs, and support for an external KMS. Is that covered?
[02:04] Maya: Yes. We have SOC2, and the private option supports external KMS via bring-your-own-key. We'll share the SOC2 report and network diagrams after the call.
[02:12] Liam: For the open models, which families are you recommending today? We've seen Llama2-based quantized variants, Mistral variants, and some of the new long-context models. Performance vs hallucination tradeoffs are our concern.
[02:28] Diego: For retrieval and tool-calling, we typically recommend models with strong instruction-following and tool interface framing — often the 13B-70B open families depending on latency/budget. For long-context, there are specialized long-window variants (e.g., 32k-mems). We also use KV cache and prefix caching to reduce cost on repeated context.
[02:48] Priya: Can you give concrete examples? We need to evaluate hallucination vs cost.
[02:53] Diego: Sure — short summary: Llama2-Chat quantized 8-bit is cheap and decent but struggles on some multilingual edge cases. Mistral-instruct tends to be stronger on few-shot instruction, lower flops for similar quality. There's also longer-context LLMs like Falcon-40B-instruct with 32k variants; trade is GPU RAM and latency. Redwood helps with quantization profiles and recommends kernels to optimize throughput.
[03:18] Arjun: Tool-calling — do you support function-calling style structured outputs? e.g., return JSON with function names and arguments to call index services?
[03:24] Maya: Yes, we support function/tool calling with streaming. Diego can go deeper on how we surface tool call metadata and retries.
[03:30] Diego: Implementation note — we support explicit function signatures and structured responses; we also provide hooks for retry policies, idempotency tokens, and automatic fallback to alternate model variants if the primary times out. For heavy tool-calling workloads the Dedicated pool with predictable throughput helps avoid throttling.
[03:49] Liam: How does prefix/KV caching work with RAG? We have many repeated patterns in prompts.
[03:55] Diego: We do automatic prefix cache for repeated tokens and KV cache for autoregressive generation. For RAG, if you canonicalize chunk ordering we can cache the tokenization of the fixed prefix. That reduces per-token compute significantly.
[04:09] Priya: About latency — 400 ms p95 is our target for short responses. Can you meet that on hosted?
[04:15] Maya: Hosted can meet that for smaller models (13B) in many regions, but at scale and under burst you may get variability. Dedicated capacity gives stronger p95 guarantees with planned throughput and can be SLA-backed. 
[04:28] Nora: What about multi-region routing? Our customers are global and we need data residency in EU and NA.
[04:34] Diego: Smart routing can pin requests by customer region, and our private deployment can be deployed into a customer VPC in target regions. We can also do hybrid — local region dedicated pools + hosted fallback.
[04:47] Arjun: Cost model — what levers should we be thinking about to reduce $/completed request?
[04:52] Diego: Batch size, quantization, context window size, and caching are the main levers. Also routing lower priority or non-sensitive queries to cheaper, smaller models. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles by workload.
[05:05] Liam: Does Redwood do automatic model fallbacks if a request times out? You mentioned variants earlier.
[05:10] Maya: Yes — policy-based fallbacks. You can define a tiered policy: primary model -> cheaper variant -> degraded shorter context with cached prefix.
[05:20] Priya: For the PoC we want: (1) 8k vs 32k latency/cost comparison, (2) tool-calling reliability under concurrency, (3) multilingual quality with FR/ES/JA. Is that feasible?
[05:31] Diego: Totally feasible. We'll propose a short benchmark plan with synthetic loads and some of your sanitized prompts. For multilingual evals we'll run BLEU/ROUGE-style checks and human review on a sample.
[05:42] Arjun: Any limits on streaming and token-level hooks? We need to show partial outputs to the UI fast.
[05:47] Diego: Streaming is supported — chunked token streaming with event hooks. You can also attach traces for observability in Console.

[05:58] -- quick pause for background noise / someone drops briefly --

[06:12] Nora: I want details on network controls and whether we can force egress through our firewall for the private deployment.
[06:18] Maya: In private/VPC mode, the control plane can be customer-controlled and egress can be restricted. We'll share the network architecture doc.
[06:26] Liam: Regarding open-source licensing — any gotchas deploying certain weights in Dedicated vs Private?
[06:31] Diego: Licensing is upstream — we'd advise on license compatibility. Private on-prem is safest for stricter licenses, but many open weights are permissive. We'll flag any Llama-derived obligations.

[06:45] Priya: Can you walk through a sample request path if we do hosted vs private for a tool-calling flow?
[06:52] Diego: Hosted: client -> Redwood API (region) -> serving runtime picks healthy node -> model generates -> tool call event returned -> Redwood logs and traces. Private: client -> (within your VPC) -> control plane points to local dedicated runtime -> model runs inside your infra, keys remain in your KMS. Latency and audit logs are more under your control in private.
[07:18] Priya: On metrics, what telemetry do we get? token breakdowns, per-route latency, per model?
[07:23] Maya: Console gives token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latencies, traces, error rates, and per-token breakdown by model and kernel. We also expose an API for exporting metrics to your observability stack.

[07:35] Liam: What about quantization — do you manage that or do we? We tried q4_0 and saw quality regressions on some tasks.
[07:43] Diego: Redwood provides recommended quantization profiles and handles kernel selection. For sensitive tasks we advise mixed strategy: keep critical models in higher-precision, push non-critical to aggressive quant. We'll include recommendations in the PoC plan.

[07:57] Arjun: Ok can we talk about an example of fallback policy for tool-calling? If the primary model returns malformed JSON, what's the approach?
[08:04] Diego: We have schema validation and optional auto-reprompt with a constrained system prompt. If malformed and retry fails, we can fall back to a different model or run a structured parser on the output. Also you can enable a 'syntactic guard' that rejects output that doesn't match function signature.

[08:24] Priya: For the PoC dataset, what format should we send prompts and expected responses in?
[08:29] Maya: CSV or JSONL with fields: prompt, expected_response, language, expected_latency_slo. For tool-calls include function signatures.

[08:38] -- timestamp jumps ahead during planning --

[24:10] Maya: Back to the model selection — given your multilingual and long-doc needs, our initial recommendation is to baseline on a 13B long-context variant and a 30-40B long-context variant. The 13B variant to hit the 400 ms p95 in hosted for simple responses; the 40B for higher-fidelity summarization with 32k windows on Dedicated.
[24:30] Liam: Does the 32k window require different hardware? We have constraints in our infra for PoC.
[24:36] Diego: Yes, 32k windows typically require GPUs with larger memory or more advanced kernel streaming; Redwood can allocate Dedicated instances with the right GPUs or run in Private with your on-prem hardware if compatible. We'll include hardware-spec guidance.
[24:51] Priya: Any rough cost delta between hosted (usaging) vs dedicated reserved? We want ballpark to evaluate.
[24:58] Maya: Hosted is pure usage pricing — good for ramping and variable loads. Dedicated is cheaper per-token at scale but requires commit. For rough numbers we'll include an example: if you're doing X tokens/day, dedicated can be 30-50% cheaper depending on utilization. We'll send a tailored estimate.

[25:18] Nora: Security questions again — log retention windows and whether logs can be disabled for sensitive flows?
[25:23] Diego: Audit logs are configurable; for private you can keep logs in your storage. For hosted we retain logs per the plan; we can route sensitive flows to private or dedicated with stricter retention rules.

[25:35] Priya: For PoC measurement, we care about hallucination rates for QA tasks. How do we measure that objectively?
[25:42] Diego: Automated metrics plus human-in-the-loop labeling. We'll run targeted evals and produce a regression report comparing models by hallucination frequency on your test set.

[26:00] Maya: Quick note on integrations: Redwood has sample SDKs and plugins for common vector stores (we've validated with Pinecone, Milvus, FAISS connectors) and we can share examples for your internal index service.
[26:12] Arjun: Are there rate limits on function calls per minute?
[26:16] Diego: In Hosted there's soft quotas that you can raise; Dedicated you control capacity. We'll show typical throttle numbers in the docs.

[26:28] -- some cross-talk, brief audio glitch --

[26:40] Priya: We will need to sign an NDA before sharing some of the data samples.
[26:44] Maya: Noted. We'll route NDA and security pack.

[26:50] Liam: One more question — model updates/rollouts. If a model variant is updated upstream, how do rollouts work? We can't have sudden quality regressions in prod.
[26:58] Maya: We have version pinning and rollout controls — canary, A/B, automatic fallback on regression alerts. Redwood Optimize ties regressions to eval suites so you can block bad versions.

[27:12] Priya: Good. On timeline we want to start a small PoC within two weeks if possible.
[27:17] Maya: Diego, can you suggest PoC dates?
[27:20] Diego: I'll propose a 2-week bench plan starting 2026-07-06, with an initial config day and then 5 days of load + qualitative evals.

[27:30] Arjun: Works for us, pending NDA.

[27:34] -- planning continues, then recaps --

[27:45] Maya: Recap — we'll send SOC2 + network diagram + sample pricing. Diego will share a PoC plan and benchmark steps. Liam to share sanitized prompts and Arjun to coordinate NDA. Next call tentatively 2026-07-07 for kickoff.

[27:59] Priya: Thanks all. Quick operational note — we may prefer Dedicated for predictability but want to evaluate hosted to start.
[28:08] Maya: That's a common path — hosted first, then commit to Dedicated after validating throughput and SLOs.

[28:16] Nora: Any blockers for us to perform the PoC?
[28:19] Diego: Primarily NDA and sanitized sample data, and a runner on your side to coordinate latency targets. Redwood can handle the rest.

[28:30] Liam: We'll also test structured tool-calls under concurrency — that was our real worry.
[28:35] Diego: We'll include concurrency scenarios in the bench.

[28:42] -- closing pleasantries --

[28:50] Maya: Thanks again, we'll follow up with the assets.
[28:53] Priya: Appreciate it.

[29:00] End of recorded portion.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap, some words garbled around kernel selection and quant names (q4_0 transcribed sometimes q forty), timestamps approximate.
